summary: A slender, long-armed octopus of tropical sand and silt flats that forages in daylight, in full view of predatory fish. Instead of just hiding, it reshapes its body and colours to impersonate other animals, including venomous ones, and appears to choose its disguise to suit the threat.

stats.range: Indo-West Pacific, from the Red Sea to New Caledonia and the Great Barrier Reef; most records from Indonesia

facts.title: Found on film first
facts.text: Scientists filming in Sulawesi and Bali described it as an octopus new to science in 2001; its formal scientific name followed in 2005.

facts.title: Dynamic mimicry
facts.text: Nine individuals were seen switching between postures and colour patterns, several clearly impersonating venomous animals that share its habitat. Biologists call this shape-shifting repertoire 'dynamic mimicry'.

facts.title: A cast of characters
facts.text: Reported guises include a lionfish (arms fanned out like spines), a banded sea snake (two arms stretched out, the rest hidden) and a flat, banded sole gliding over the sand.

facts.title: Choosing the right disguise
facts.text: Observers suggest the octopus picks a model to fit the threat: one harassed by damselfish turned into a 'sea snake', a predator of damselfish. How deliberate this choice is remains under study.

facts.title: Mud, not reef
facts.text: Unlike most octopuses that shelter on reefs, it lives on open sand and silt, often near river mouths, jetting just above the bottom to search burrows for prey.

references.title: Dynamic mimicry in an Indo-Malayan octopus (Norman, Finn & Tregenza 2001, Proc. R. Soc. B)

image.alt: A mimic octopus with bold brown-and-white banded arms spread over dark sand, its small eyes raised on top of its head
image.caption: Mimic octopus on a sandy bottom at Anilao, Philippines
image.creator: Rickard Zerpe

notes: Specific mimicry models (lionfish, sea snake, sole), size, depth, range and IUCN status come from Wikipedia, which cites Norman & Hochberg 2005, Hanlon et al. 2008 and IUCN (Allcock 2019); the primary papers and IUCN site could not be fetched (403/JS). The 'choice of disguise' fact is framed as a hypothesis, as in Norman et al. 2001 ('our observations suggest'). Close relative Wunderpus photogenicus looks similar; the chosen photo is labelled T. mimicus by the photographer.
